stem: A practitioner notes that the pulse is wiry and forceful only at the guan (middle) position of the patient's right wrist, while all other positions are normal. Under the standard position-organ correspondence, this finding most directly reflects which organ?

options.A: Spleen and Stomach
options.B: Liver and Gallbladder
options.C: Lung and Large Intestine
options.D: Kidney and Bladder

explanation: In the standard correspondence used by Cheng Xinnong and Maciocia, the right wrist reads Lung (cun), Spleen/Stomach (guan), and Kidney (chi), while the left wrist reads Heart (cun), Liver/Gallbladder (guan), and Kidney (chi). A change confined to the right guan therefore points to the Middle Burner, Spleen and Stomach.

distractorExplanations.B: Liver and Gallbladder are read at the guan position of the left wrist, not the right. The learner has confused the two sides.
distractorExplanations.C: Lung and Large Intestine are read at the right cun (distal) position, not the guan.
distractorExplanations.D: Kidney and Bladder are read at the chi (proximal) position on both wrists.

learningObjective: Identify the organ correspondence of each radial pulse position on the left and right wrists.

references.source: Cheng Xinnong, Chinese Acupuncture and Moxibustion, 4th ed.
Maciocia, Diagnosis in Chinese Medicine, 2nd ed.

stem: A 55-year-old patient reports palpitations and poor sleep. The practitioner wishes to palpate the position that most directly reflects the Heart. Which position is most appropriate?

options.A: Right cun (distal) position
options.B: Left guan (middle) position
options.C: Left cun (distal) position
options.D: Right chi (proximal) position

explanation: The Heart (with the Small Intestine) is read at the cun position of the left wrist. Cun positions reflect the Upper Burner organs, with the left side assigned to the Heart and the right side to the Lung.

distractorExplanations.B: The left guan reflects the Liver and Gallbladder, the Middle Burner organs on the left.
distractorExplanations.D: The right chi reflects the Kidney (often described as Kidney Yang or Ming Men), a Lower Burner position.

learningObjective: Identify the pulse position corresponding to the Heart.

stem: A normal pulse is said to have Stomach Qi, Spirit (Shen), and root. Which palpatory finding best demonstrates that a pulse has root?

options.A: The beat is regular and even in rhythm at all three positions
options.B: The beat remains perceptible at the chi positions on deep pressure
options.C: The beat is gentle, calm, and of moderate rate at the middle level
options.D: The beat arrives and departs smoothly with a soft, relaxed quality

explanation: Root refers to the Kidney and Yuan Qi as the foundation of the pulse. It is demonstrated when the pulse can still be felt at the chi (proximal) positions under heavy pressure. Stomach Qi is shown by a gentle, moderate, relaxed quality, and Spirit by softness with regular rhythm.

distractorExplanations.A: Regular, even rhythm is a feature of Spirit (Shen) in the pulse, not root.
distractorExplanations.C: A gentle, calm, moderate pulse at the middle level describes Stomach Qi, not root.
distractorExplanations.D: Smooth arrival and departure with softness describes Stomach Qi and Spirit, not the Kidney root felt at the chi position.

learningObjective: Identify the three qualities of a normal pulse and the finding that demonstrates root.

stem: When pulse rate is measured against the practitioner's own breathing, a pulse that is classified as slow is best defined as one that beats how many times per complete breath?

options.A: Seven or more beats per breath
options.B: Six beats per breath
options.C: Four to five beats per breath
options.D: Fewer than four beats per breath

explanation: The normal pulse is four to five beats per practitioner breath (roughly 60-90 per minute). A slow pulse is fewer than four beats per breath (under about 60 per minute); a rapid pulse is more than five beats per breath (over about 90 per minute).

distractorExplanations.A: Seven or more beats per breath describes an extremely rapid (racing) pulse, not a slow one.
distractorExplanations.B: Six beats per breath is a rapid pulse.
distractorExplanations.C: Four to five beats per breath is the normal rate, and a relaxed four-beat pulse is the slowed-down (moderate) pulse rather than the slow pulse.

learningObjective: Define slow, normal, and rapid pulse rates in beats per practitioner breath.

stem: A healthy 28-year-old patient is examined in early spring. The pulse is slightly wiry at all positions but soft, regular, and of normal rate, and the patient has no symptoms. Which interpretation of this pulse is most appropriate?

options.A: A normal seasonal variation reflecting the rising Qi of spring
options.B: An early sign of Liver Qi stagnation requiring treatment
options.C: A sign of Cold obstructing the channels
options.D: A sign of Phlegm accumulating in the Middle Burner

explanation: The classics describe seasonal pulse variations in a healthy person: slightly wiry in spring, slightly overflowing in summer, slightly floating in autumn, and slightly deep in winter. A mildly wiry pulse that retains softness, regularity, and Stomach Qi in a symptom-free patient in spring is normal, reflecting the Liver and the rising Wood Qi of the season.

distractorExplanations.B: Liver Qi stagnation would be accompanied by symptoms such as hypochondrial distension, irritability, or sighing, and the wiry quality would be more pronounced and harder, lacking softness.
distractorExplanations.C: Cold produces a tight pulse (taut and twisted like a rope), and the patient would show cold signs; a soft, slightly wiry pulse in a healthy person is seasonal.
distractorExplanations.D: Phlegm gives a slippery pulse, not a wiry one, and would be accompanied by symptoms such as chest oppression or a greasy coating.

learningObjective: Recognize normal seasonal variations of the pulse in a healthy patient.

references.source: Maciocia, Diagnosis in Chinese Medicine, 2nd ed.

stem: A pulse is felt clearly with light finger pressure at the superficial level and becomes weaker when the fingers press toward the bone. In a patient who has just developed chills, sneezing, and a headache, this pulse most commonly indicates which of the following?

options.A: An interior pattern of Excess
options.B: Yin deficiency with floating of Yang
options.C: An exterior pattern from invasion of a pathogenic factor
options.D: Retention of Phlegm in the chest

explanation: A pulse that is strongest at the superficial level and weakens on pressure is the floating pulse. In the setting of acute chills, sneezing, and headache, it reflects Wei Qi rising to the surface to fight an exterior pathogenic factor, so it indicates an exterior pattern.

distractorExplanations.A: Interior patterns of Excess produce a deep and forceful pulse, because the pathogenic factor is in the interior rather than drawing Qi to the surface.
distractorExplanations.B: A floating pulse can occur in Yin deficiency, but it is then floating and empty in a chronic patient without acute exterior symptoms; the acute presentation here identifies an exterior invasion.
distractorExplanations.D: Phlegm in the chest gives a slippery pulse, and the symptoms would include chest oppression and sputum rather than acute chills and sneezing.

learningObjective: Identify the floating pulse and its primary clinical significance.

references.source: Cheng Xinnong, Chinese Acupuncture and Moxibustion, 4th ed.

stem: A 31-year-old woman is seen two days after a delivery complicated by heavy bleeding. She is pale, dizzy, and faint. The pulse is felt at the superficial level, is large and soft, and feels empty in the center, like pressing the stalk of a scallion. Which pulse quality best describes this finding?

options.A: Scattered pulse
options.B: Hollow pulse
options.C: Floating pulse
options.D: Soggy pulse

explanation: The hollow (kong) pulse is floating, large, and soft, with an empty center like a scallion stalk, firm at the edges and absent in the middle. It classically appears after severe loss of Blood, when the vessels are suddenly under-filled while Yang has not yet collapsed. The recent hemorrhage, pallor, and dizziness confirm it.

distractorExplanations.A: The scattered pulse is floating and large but has no distinct boundaries, disappears on slight pressure, and is irregular; it indicates collapse of Yuan Qi, not simply acute Blood loss, and lacks the scallion-stalk emptiness in the center.
distractorExplanations.C: A simple floating pulse is felt superficially and weakens on pressure but does not have the large, hollow-centered feel; it chiefly indicates an exterior pattern, which this patient does not have.
distractorExplanations.D: The soggy pulse is floating but thin and soft, like cotton on water; it is small rather than large and hollow, and indicates Dampness or deficiency rather than acute hemorrhage.

learningObjective: Differentiate the hollow pulse from the floating, scattered, and soggy pulses.

distinction.key: The hollow pulse is large with an empty center but clear edges after Blood loss; the scattered pulse has no boundaries, vanishes on light pressure, and is irregular in Yuan Qi collapse.

stem: An 84-year-old patient with a long-standing chronic illness is examined during an acute deterioration. The pulse is superficial, large, and without distinct edges; it vanishes with slight pressure and its beats are irregular in strength and rhythm. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.A: Acute loss of Blood with under-filling of the vessels
options.B: Exterior invasion of Wind-Heat in a deficient patient
options.C: Interior Heat driving Qi and Blood outward
options.D: Dissipation of Yuan Qi with Yang about to collapse

explanation: This is the scattered (san) pulse: floating, large, rootless, with blurred boundaries, disappearing on light pressure and irregular in rhythm. It signifies that Yuan Qi is scattering and Yang is on the verge of collapse, a critical sign in the elderly or in late-stage chronic illness.

distractorExplanations.A: Acute Blood loss gives the hollow pulse, which is large but keeps distinct edges with an empty center; there is no bleeding history here, and the irregular rootless quality points to Qi collapse.
distractorExplanations.B: Exterior Wind-Heat gives a floating and rapid pulse with definite edges, together with fever, sore throat, and aversion to wind; a pulse that vanishes on slight pressure with irregularity is a sign of collapse, not invasion.
distractorExplanations.C: Interior Heat produces a pulse that is forceful and often overflowing or full; a forceless pulse with no root is the opposite of an Excess Heat pulse.

learningObjective: Identify the scattered pulse and recognize it as a sign of critical Yuan Qi collapse.

distinction.key: A scattered pulse has no boundaries, no root, and irregular rhythm; a hollow pulse is large with clear edges and an empty center after Blood loss.

references.source: Maciocia, Diagnosis in Chinese Medicine, 2nd ed.

stem: A 47-year-old patient presents with sudden severe, cramping abdominal pain, cold limbs, and a pale complexion. The pulse can be found only by pressing to the bone and pushing the tendon aside; it is completely absent at the superficial and middle levels. Which pulse quality best describes this finding?

options.A: Hidden pulse
options.B: Deep pulse
options.C: Firm pulse
options.D: Weak pulse

explanation: The hidden (fu) pulse lies deeper than the deep pulse: it is felt only by pressing to the bone and moving the tendon aside. It indicates severe Cold or pathogenic obstruction closing off Yang Qi in the interior, typically with violent pain or syncope, and may also signal collapse of Yang. The acute severe pain and cold limbs fit this picture.

distractorExplanations.B: The deep pulse is felt at the deep level with heavy pressure but is still obtainable at that level without pushing the tendon aside; the hidden pulse is a further degree of depth reserved for severe obstruction or collapse.
distractorExplanations.C: The firm pulse is deep but also large, wiry, long, and forceful, and is felt firmly at the deep level rather than being nearly absent; it indicates interior Cold with accumulation such as masses.
distractorExplanations.D: The weak pulse is deep, thin, and soft, but is readily felt at the deep level; it indicates chronic Qi and Blood or Yang deficiency rather than an acute closed-off state.

learningObjective: Differentiate the hidden pulse from the deep, firm, and weak pulses.

distinction.key: A deep pulse is felt at the deep level with heavy pressure; a hidden pulse requires pressing to the bone and displacing the tendon, and signals severe Cold obstruction or collapse.

stem: A 58-year-old man reports a long-standing fixed lower abdominal mass with cold, dull pain that improves with warmth. His pulse is deep, large, long, wiry, and forceful, and keeps its force under heavy pressure. Which pulse quality best describes this finding?

options.A: Hidden pulse
options.B: Deep pulse
options.C: Firm pulse
options.D: Tight pulse

explanation: The firm (lao) pulse is deep, large, long, wiry, and forceful; it is immovable under pressure and is found only at the deep level. It indicates interior Cold with accumulation of Excess, such as abdominal masses or hernial pain. The chronic fixed mass with cold pain matches this significance.

distractorExplanations.A: The hidden pulse is nearly absent, obtainable only by pushing the tendon aside at the bone; a large, forceful pulse at the deep level is the opposite in strength.
distractorExplanations.B: A deep pulse is defined by depth alone; it may be forceful or forceless. The combination of deep with large, long, wiry, and forceful has its own name, the firm pulse.
distractorExplanations.D: The tight pulse feels like a twisted rope and is defined by tension rather than depth; it is found at any level and indicates Cold with pain, but lacks the deep, large, long, immovable quality.

learningObjective: Identify the firm pulse and differentiate it from the deep, hidden, and tight pulses.

distinction.key: Both lie at the deep level, but the firm pulse is large, long, wiry, and forceful under pressure, while the hidden pulse is barely obtainable even at the bone.

stem: A 39-year-old patient reports a heavy sensation in the body and limbs, loose stools, and a feeling of fullness after meals. The tongue has a greasy white coating. The pulse beats about four times per practitioner breath and feels relaxed and loose, with a slightly slippery quality. Which pulse quality best describes the rate and feel of this pulse?

options.A: Slow pulse
options.B: Slowed-down (moderate) pulse
options.C: Soggy pulse
options.D: Weak pulse

explanation: The slowed-down or moderate (huan) pulse beats about four times per breath, slower than normal but faster than the slow pulse, with a loose, relaxed quality. When pathological, it indicates Dampness or Spleen deficiency, which the heaviness, loose stools, and greasy coating support.

distractorExplanations.A: The slow pulse is fewer than four beats per breath (below about 60 per minute) and indicates Cold; a four-beat relaxed pulse is slowed-down, not slow.
distractorExplanations.C: The soggy pulse is defined by depth and width (floating, thin, soft), not by rate; the stem describes a relaxed four-beat pulse, which is a rate category.
distractorExplanations.D: The weak pulse is deep, thin, and forceless; the stem does not describe a deep or forceless pulse but a relaxed, moderately slow one.

learningObjective: Differentiate the slowed-down (moderate) pulse from the slow pulse and state its significance.

distinction.key: The slowed-down pulse is about four beats per breath and relaxed (Dampness or Spleen deficiency); the slow pulse is fewer than four beats per breath and indicates Cold.

references.source: Maciocia, Diagnosis in Chinese Medicine, 2nd ed.

stem: A 42-year-old patient develops severe, cramping lower abdominal pain after eating a large quantity of ice cream on a cold day. The pain is worse with pressure and better with a hot pack. The pulse is slow and forceful. Which interpretation of the pulse is most appropriate?

options.A: Cold from Yang deficiency in the interior
options.B: Heat obstructing the flow of Qi
options.C: Dampness slowing the circulation of Qi
options.D: Full Cold obstructing the interior

explanation: A slow pulse indicates Cold. Its strength differentiates the type: slow and forceful indicates Full (Excess) Cold, in which a Cold pathogenic factor obstructs Yang Qi, whereas slow and forceless indicates Empty Cold from Yang deficiency. The acute onset after cold food, pain worse with pressure, and the forceful quality all confirm Full Cold.

distractorExplanations.A: Yang deficiency produces a slow but forceless pulse and chronic, dull pain that likes pressure; the forceful pulse and pain worse with pressure identify Excess.
distractorExplanations.B: Heat produces a rapid pulse, not a slow one, and pain from Heat would be relieved by cold rather than a hot pack.
distractorExplanations.C: Dampness gives a slowed-down or soggy pulse, often with slipperiness, together with heaviness and a greasy coating; it does not produce a forceful slow pulse with acute cramping pain after cold food.

learningObjective: Interpret the strength of a slow pulse to differentiate Full Cold from Empty Cold.

distinction.key: Slow and forceful is Full Cold; slow and forceless is Empty Cold from Yang deficiency.

references.source: Cheng Xinnong, Chinese Acupuncture and Moxibustion, 4th ed.

stem: A pulse is rapid, beating more than five times per practitioner breath, and periodically misses a beat at irregular intervals. Which pulse quality best describes this finding?

options.A: Hasty pulse
options.B: Knotted pulse
options.C: Intermittent pulse
options.D: Moving pulse

explanation: The hasty (cu) pulse is rapid with irregularly missed beats. It indicates Heat with stagnation of Qi, Blood, Phlegm, or Food, or in deficient patients an exhaustion of Zang Qi with Heat. The two defining features are rapid rate and irregular pauses.

distractorExplanations.B: The knotted pulse also has irregularly missed beats, but it is slow rather than rapid, and indicates Cold with stagnation or Yin Excess.
distractorExplanations.C: The intermittent pulse misses beats at regular intervals with a longer pause and is not defined by rapidity; it indicates exhaustion of the Zang organs, especially the Heart.
distractorExplanations.D: The moving pulse is rapid but has no missed beats; it is short, slippery, and bean-like, most evident at the guan position, and indicates fright or pain.

learningObjective: Differentiate the hasty pulse from the knotted, intermittent, and moving pulses.

distinction.key: Both miss beats irregularly; hasty is rapid (Heat with stagnation), knotted is slow (Cold with stagnation).

stem: A 26-year-old woman is seen the morning after a frightening car accident in which she was uninjured. She is anxious with palpitations. Her pulse is rapid, slippery, and short, beating like a rolling bean, most clearly at the guan positions. Which pulse quality best describes this finding?

options.A: Slippery pulse
options.B: Hasty pulse
options.C: Moving pulse
options.D: Short pulse

explanation: The moving (dong) pulse is short, slippery, rapid, and forceful, felt like a bean rolling under the finger, typically most evident at the guan position. It indicates fright, severe pain, or (in women) pregnancy. The acute fright with palpitations matches it.

distractorExplanations.A: The slippery pulse is smooth and rolling like pearls but is felt across all positions and is not short or confined to the guan; it indicates Phlegm, Dampness, Food retention, or pregnancy.
distractorExplanations.B: The hasty pulse is rapid with irregularly missed beats; the stem describes no missed beats.
distractorExplanations.D: The short pulse is defined only by its reduced length (felt mainly at the guan), and indicates Qi deficiency or stagnation; the combination of short with slippery, rapid, and bean-like is the moving pulse.

learningObjective: Identify the moving pulse and differentiate it from the slippery, hasty, and short pulses.

distinction.key: The moving pulse is short, rapid, and bean-like at the guan (fright, pain); the slippery pulse rolls smoothly across all positions (Phlegm, Damp, Food, pregnancy).

stem: A 52-year-old woman reports night sweats, a feeling of heat in the palms and soles in the evening, dry mouth at night, and a slight afternoon flush. The tongue is red with a peeled coating. The pulse is rapid and thin. Which interpretation of the pulse is most appropriate?

options.A: Full Heat in the Qi level injuring Body Fluids
options.B: Empty Heat arising from Yin deficiency
options.C: Phlegm-Heat obstructing the vessels
options.D: Blood deficiency with Blood failing to nourish the vessels

explanation: A rapid pulse indicates Heat; its width and strength tell the type. Rapid and forceful (often overflowing or full) indicates Full Heat, while rapid and thin indicates Empty Heat from Yin deficiency, because deficient Yin fails to fill the vessels while deficiency Heat speeds the rate. Night sweats, five-palm heat, and a red peeled tongue confirm Yin deficiency.

distractorExplanations.A: Full Heat in the Qi level gives a rapid and overflowing or full pulse with high fever, great thirst, and a yellow coating, not a thin pulse with a peeled tongue.
distractorExplanations.C: Phlegm-Heat gives a rapid and slippery pulse with a greasy yellow coating, not a thin pulse with a peeled coating.
distractorExplanations.D: Blood deficiency alone gives a thin or choppy pulse without rapidity, with a pale tongue; the rapid rate and red tongue indicate Heat from Yin deficiency.

learningObjective: Interpret the combination of rapid and thin pulse as Empty Heat from Yin deficiency.

distinction.key: Rapid and forceful (overflowing or full) is Full Heat; rapid and thin is Empty Heat from Yin deficiency.

references.source: Maciocia, The Foundations of Chinese Medicine, 3rd ed.

stem: A 76-year-old patient with advanced chronic illness has cold limbs, profuse cold sweat, and a barely audible voice. The pulse is extremely fine and soft, so faint that it is almost imperceptible and seems about to disappear under the fingers. Which pulse quality best describes this finding?

options.A: Thin pulse
options.B: Weak pulse
options.C: Soggy pulse
options.D: Minute pulse

explanation: The minute (wei, faint) pulse is extremely thin and soft, so indistinct that it seems on the verge of vanishing. It indicates severe deficiency of Yang Qi, or collapse of Yang, with Qi and Blood exhausted; the cold sweat, cold limbs, and feeble voice confirm Yang collapse.

distractorExplanations.A: The thin (thready) pulse is fine like a thread but remains distinct and clearly felt; it indicates Blood or Yin deficiency, or Dampness, and is not a sign of collapse.
distractorExplanations.B: The weak pulse is deep, thin, and forceless but is still clearly obtainable at the deep level; it indicates chronic Qi and Blood or Yang deficiency rather than an imminent collapse.
distractorExplanations.C: The soggy pulse is floating, thin, and soft, like cotton on water; it is clearly perceptible at the superficial level and indicates Dampness or deficiency, not collapse.

learningObjective: Differentiate the minute pulse from the thin, weak, and soggy pulses.

distinction.key: A thin pulse is fine but distinct; a minute pulse is so faint it seems about to vanish, signalling Yang collapse.

stem: A pulse is felt at the superficial level, is somewhat large, but is forceless, and it becomes empty and indistinct when the fingers press to the deep level. Which pulse quality best describes this finding, and what does it most commonly indicate?

options.A: Empty pulse; deficiency of Qi and Blood
options.B: Weak pulse; deficiency of Yang
options.C: Hollow pulse; acute loss of Blood
options.D: Floating pulse; invasion of an exterior pathogenic factor

explanation: The empty (xu, deficient) pulse is felt at the superficial level, is large and soft, forceless, and empties on deep pressure. It indicates deficiency of Qi and Blood: Qi is insufficient to drive the pulse and Blood insufficient to fill the vessels. Its defining features are superficial location and lack of force.

distractorExplanations.B: The weak pulse is deep, thin, and soft; it is the forceless pulse found at the deep level, whereas the empty pulse is found at the superficial level. The learner has confused the levels at which forceless pulses are felt.
distractorExplanations.C: The hollow pulse is also superficial and large, but it keeps firm edges around an empty center like a scallion stalk, and follows acute hemorrhage; the plain empty pulse is uniformly soft and forceless.
distractorExplanations.D: The floating pulse of an exterior invasion is superficial but is usually forceful, because Wei Qi is contending with the pathogenic factor; forcelessness is the sign of deficiency.

learningObjective: Define the empty pulse and differentiate it from the weak, hollow, and floating pulses.

distinction.key: Both are forceless, but the empty pulse is felt at the superficial level and the weak pulse at the deep level.

stem: A 68-year-old man reports years of fatigue, cold hands and feet, a bright-pale face, and loose stools in the early morning. The tongue is pale and swollen with a thin white coating. options.B: Minute pulse
options.C: Weak pulse

distractorExplanations.D: The hidden pulse is obtainable only by pressing to the bone and displacing the tendon, in acute severe Cold obstruction or collapse; it is not a chronic deficiency pulse found at the usual deep level.

learningObjective: Identify the weak pulse and link it to chronic Yang deficiency.

stem: A 35-year-old man develops severe epigastric pain and chills after working outdoors in freezing rain. The pain is intense and unrelieved by position. The pulse is forceful and taut, with a side-to-side tension that feels like a twisted rope under the fingers. Which pulse quality best describes this finding?

options.A: Wiry pulse
options.B: Tight pulse
options.C: Long pulse
options.D: Full pulse

explanation: The tight (jin) pulse is forceful and taut, with a twisting, rope-like tension that shifts under the fingers. It indicates Cold, either exterior or interior, and pain. Exposure to cold with severe pain and chills matches the tight pulse exactly.

distractorExplanations.C: The long pulse is defined by extending beyond the cun and chi positions; it does not describe tension or twisting and, when soft, is a normal pulse.
distractorExplanations.D: The full pulse is large and forceful at all three levels and indicates Excess, commonly with Heat; it lacks the taut, rope-like quality specific to Cold.

learningObjective: Differentiate the tight pulse from the wiry, long, and full pulses.

distinction.key: Tight feels like a twisted rope with side-to-side tension (Cold, pain); wiry feels like a straight guitar string (Liver, pain, Phlegm).

options.A: Soggy pulse; Dampness or deficiency of Blood and Yin
options.B: Slippery pulse; Phlegm or retention of Food
options.C: Floating pulse; invasion of an exterior pathogenic factor
options.D: Thin pulse; deficiency of Blood

explanation: The soggy (ru, soft) pulse combines three features: floating, thin, and soft, like cotton floating on water. It indicates Dampness (which prevents the pulse from sinking while weakening it) or deficiency of Blood, Yin, or Essence. All three features together define it.

distractorExplanations.D: The thin pulse is fine but can be felt at any level and is distinct; the soggy pulse adds the superficial level and softness.

learningObjective: Define the soggy pulse and differentiate it from the slippery, floating, and thin pulses.

distinction.key: Soggy is floating, thin, and soft like cotton on water; slippery is smooth and rolling like pearls, of normal width, felt at all levels.

stem: A healthy 29-year-old woman reports eight weeks of amenorrhea with mild nausea in the mornings. She has no digestive complaints otherwise, no cough, and a tongue with a thin white coating. options.A: Phlegm-Damp accumulating in the Middle Burner
options.B: Retention of Food in the Stomach
options.C: A physiological pulse consistent with pregnancy
options.D: Damp-Heat in the Lower Burner

explanation: The slippery pulse indicates Phlegm, Dampness, or retention of Food when pathological, but a slippery and slightly rapid pulse in a healthy woman of childbearing age is also the classical sign of pregnancy, reflecting the abundance of Qi and Blood nourishing the fetus. stem: A 61-year-old patient with chronic chest oppression and a purplish tongue has a pulse that is slow, fewer than four beats per practitioner breath, and misses a beat at irregular intervals. Which pulse quality best describes this finding?

options.A: Choppy pulse
options.B: Intermittent pulse
options.C: Hasty pulse
options.D: Knotted pulse

explanation: The knotted (jie) pulse is slow with irregularly missed beats. It indicates Cold with obstruction, such as Qi or Blood stagnation, Phlegm, or accumulated Yin Cold; when forceless it indicates deficiency of Qi and Blood with stasis. The chronic chest oppression and purplish tongue fit Cold and Blood stasis obstructing the Heart.

distractorExplanations.C: The hasty pulse misses beats irregularly but is rapid, indicating Heat with stagnation; this pulse is slow.

learningObjective: Differentiate the knotted pulse from the choppy, intermittent, and hasty pulses.

distinction.key: Knotted misses beats irregularly and is slow; choppy is rough and uneven in flow but keeps its rhythm.

stem: A 72-year-old woman reports palpitations, shortness of breath on slight exertion, and exhaustion. Her pulse is of moderate rate but stops at regular intervals, every fifth beat, with a pause that is noticeably prolonged before the rhythm resumes. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.A: Heat agitating the Heart with stagnation of Qi and Blood
options.B: Exhaustion of Zang organ Qi, particularly of the Heart
options.C: Cold accumulating with obstruction of Qi and Blood
options.D: Wind stirring internally from Liver Yang rising

explanation: The intermittent (dai) pulse misses beats at regular intervals with a longer pause, and the rate is not necessarily rapid or slow. distractorExplanations.D: Liver Yang rising with internal Wind gives a wiry, often rapid pulse with dizziness, headache, or tremor, not a regularly pausing pulse with exhaustion.

learningObjective: Identify the intermittent pulse and its significance of Zang Qi exhaustion.

distinction.key: Intermittent pauses at regular intervals with a long pause (Zang Qi exhaustion); knotted pauses irregularly and is slow (Cold with stagnation).

stem: A 44-year-old woman reports stabbing, fixed lower abdominal pain that is worse during menstruation, with dark menstrual blood containing clots. The tongue is purple with distended sublingual veins. The pulse is choppy and forceful, uneven like a knife scraping bamboo. Which interpretation of the choppy pulse is most appropriate?

options.A: Blood stasis obstructing the vessels
options.B: Blood deficiency failing to fill the vessels
options.C: Essence deficiency failing to nourish the vessels
options.D: Dampness slowing the flow in the vessels

explanation: The choppy (se) pulse is rough and uneven, like a knife scraping bamboo. Its strength decides its meaning: choppy and forceful indicates Blood stasis (or stagnation of Qi, Phlegm, or Food) obstructing the vessels, whereas choppy and forceless indicates deficiency of Blood or Essence. Fixed stabbing pain, clotted dark menses, and a purple tongue with distended sublingual veins confirm Blood stasis.

distractorExplanations.D: Dampness produces a soggy, slippery, or slowed-down pulse with heaviness and a greasy coating, not a forceful choppy pulse with a purple tongue.

learningObjective: Interpret the strength of a choppy pulse to differentiate Blood stasis from Blood or Essence deficiency.

distinction.key: A choppy and forceful pulse indicates Blood stasis; a choppy and forceless pulse indicates Blood or Essence deficiency.

stem: A 33-year-old man has had a high fever for two days with profuse sweating, great thirst for cold drinks, a red face, and a red tongue with a dry yellow coating. The pulse is large and forceful, arriving like a surging wave and then departing with less strength. Which pulse quality best describes this finding?

options.A: Full pulse
options.B: Wiry pulse
options.C: Overflowing pulse
options.D: Long pulse

explanation: The overflowing (hong, flooding) pulse is large and forceful, arriving with a surge and departing with diminished force, like a wave. It indicates exuberant Heat, classically Heat in the Qi level or Yang Ming, with the four big signs of high fever, profuse sweating, great thirst, and a big pulse. This patient shows exactly that picture.

distractorExplanations.D: The long pulse extends beyond the normal positions and may be normal when soft; it is defined by length, not by surging force.

learningObjective: Differentiate the overflowing pulse from the full, wiry, and long pulses.

options.B: Full pulse
options.C: Firm pulse
options.D: Tight pulse

stem: A 24-year-old patient presents with one day of chills, mild fever, absence of sweating, occipital headache, and generalized body aches. The tongue has a thin white coating. The pulse is floating and tight. Which interpretation of this pulse combination is most appropriate?

options.A: Exterior Wind-Heat
options.B: Exterior deficiency with Wei Qi failing to consolidate
options.C: Interior Cold with pain
options.D: Exterior Wind-Cold

explanation: A floating pulse indicates the exterior; a tight pulse indicates Cold. Floating and tight together therefore indicate exterior Wind-Cold. stem: A 63-year-old woman reports chronic low back coldness and pain that improves with warmth, frequent pale urination, cold feet, and a lack of energy. The tongue is pale, swollen, and wet. The pulse is deep, slow, and weak. Which interpretation of this pulse combination is most appropriate?

options.A: Interior Empty Cold from Yang deficiency
options.B: Interior Full Cold from invasion of Cold
options.C: Interior Dampness obstructing the Yang
options.D: Interior Blood stasis from Cold congealing

explanation: Deep indicates the interior, slow indicates Cold, and weak (forceless) indicates deficiency. Together they indicate interior Empty Cold, that is Yang deficiency failing to warm the body. distractorExplanations.C: Dampness gives a slippery, soggy, or slowed-down pulse with heaviness and a greasy coating; a slow and weak pulse with cold signs indicates Yang deficiency.
distractorExplanations.D: Blood stasis gives a choppy or wiry pulse with fixed stabbing pain and a purple tongue; the pale tongue and forceless pulse rule it out.

learningObjective: Interpret the deep-slow-weak pulse combination as interior Empty Cold.

distinction.key: Deep-slow-weak is Empty Cold (Yang deficiency); deep-slow-forceful or tight is Full Cold.

stem: A 46-year-old man reports dizziness with a heavy head, a bitter taste, chest oppression with sticky yellow sputum, irritability, and restless sleep. options.D: Liver Yin deficiency with Empty Heat

stem: A 37-year-old woman reports spontaneous daytime sweating, aversion to wind, frequent colds, fatigue, and shortness of breath on exertion. The tongue is pale with a thin white coating. The pulse is floating and empty, forceless at the superficial level and vanishing on deeper pressure. Which interpretation of this pulse combination is most appropriate?

options.A: Exterior Wind-Cold constraining the surface
options.B: Lung Qi deficiency with Wei Qi failing to consolidate the exterior
options.C: Yin deficiency with Yang floating upward
options.D: Heat in the Lung injuring the Body Fluids

explanation: A floating pulse ordinarily suggests the exterior, but when it is also empty (forceless and vanishing on pressure) it indicates deficiency rather than invasion: Qi is too weak to hold the pulse in and the Yang floats. With spontaneous sweating, aversion to wind, frequent colds, fatigue, and a pale tongue, this is Lung Qi deficiency with Wei Qi failing to consolidate the exterior.

distractorExplanations.C: Yin deficiency with floating Yang gives a floating-empty pulse that is also rapid or thin, with a red peeled tongue, night sweats, and heat sensations; the pale tongue and daytime sweating point to Qi deficiency.
distractorExplanations.D: Lung Heat gives a rapid and forceful pulse with cough, yellow sputum, and a red tongue, none of which are present.

learningObjective: Interpret the floating-empty pulse combination as Qi deficiency with failure to consolidate the exterior.

distinction.key: Floating-empty with spontaneous sweating is exterior deficiency (Lung Qi); floating-tight with no sweating is exterior Excess (Wind-Cold).

stem: A 70-year-old man with a long chronic illness presents with a flushed red face, a sensation of heat, thirst, and agitation. However, he wants only small sips of warm drinks, his limbs are cold, and he prefers to be covered. The tongue is pale. The pulse is deep, slow, and forceless. Which approach to the conflicting findings is most appropriate?

options.A: Follow the symptoms and treat Full Heat, because the red face and thirst are the chief complaints
options.B: Treat Heat and Cold simultaneously, because the findings indicate a mixed pattern
options.C: Follow the symptoms and treat Empty Heat from Yin deficiency
options.D: Follow the pulse and treat interior Cold, because the heat signs are deceptive

explanation: When the pulse and symptoms conflict, the practitioner must decide which reflects the true nature of the disease. Here the heat signs are false: the thirst is for small sips of warm drinks, the limbs are cold, the patient seeks covering, and the tongue is pale. The deep, slow, forceless pulse reveals the true condition, Yang deficiency with Cold in the interior driving deficient Yang to the surface (True Cold with False Heat). The pulse is followed and the symptoms disregarded.

distractorExplanations.A: Treating Full Heat would further damage Yang. The red face and thirst are the false exterior appearance of True Cold; Full Heat would show a rapid, forceful pulse and a red tongue with desire for cold drinks.
distractorExplanations.B: This is a true-false presentation produced by a single mechanism, not a genuine mixed Heat-Cold pattern; treating both would still clear a Heat that does not exist.
distractorExplanations.C: Empty Heat from Yin deficiency would show a thin, rapid pulse and a red peeled tongue; the slow forceless pulse and pale tongue exclude it.

learningObjective: Decide when to follow the pulse rather than the symptoms in a True Cold with False Heat presentation.

distinction.key: A forceless slow pulse with a pale tongue and thirst for warm sips reveals that the red face and heat sensation are false; the pulse is followed.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents one day after a large, heavy meal with marked epigastric and abdominal distension, pain that is worse with pressure, sour foul belching, and no bowel movement. The tongue has a thick greasy coating. Unexpectedly, the pulse is deep and thin rather than forceful. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.B: Follow the pulse and treat deficiency of Qi and Blood
options.C: Follow the pulse and treat Yang deficiency with Cold accumulation
options.D: Treat deficiency first and the obstruction afterward

explanation: When severe accumulation of Food or stagnation of Qi obstructs the interior, Qi and Blood cannot reach the vessels freely and the pulse may appear deep and thin despite an Excess condition. stem: A 59-year-old woman reports several years of dull low back ache, weak knees, nocturia, and tinnitus. options.B: Kidney deficiency with weakening of the root of the pulse
options.C: Spleen Qi deficiency failing to generate Blood
options.D: Liver Qi stagnation obstructing the Lower Burner

stem: A 48-year-old patient reports chronic abdominal distension and dull pain. On palpation the abdomen is soft, and the patient says the discomfort feels better when the practitioner presses on it and when a warm hand rests on the area. stem: A 51-year-old woman reports lower abdominal pain. On palpation, a soft mass is found that moves when pushed, is sometimes present and sometimes absent, and is associated with pain that shifts in location and improves after passing gas. Which interpretation of this mass is most appropriate?

options.D: Cold congealing into a firm accumulation

stem: A 43-year-old woman reports distension and discomfort under the ribs on both sides, worse with emotional stress, with frequent sighing and a wiry pulse. On palpation there is resistance and tenderness under the costal margins, with no mass. Which interpretation of the subcostal finding is most appropriate?

options.A: Liver Qi stagnation obstructing the hypochondrium
options.B: Liver Blood deficiency failing to nourish the sinews
options.C: Phlegm-Fluids accumulating in the chest
options.D: Spleen Qi deficiency with sinking of Qi

explanation: The hypochondriac region beneath the costal margins is traversed by the Liver and Gallbladder channels. Subcostal resistance and tenderness on palpation, with distension that worsens with stress, sighing, and a wiry pulse, indicate Liver Qi stagnation; the same finding appears in Shao Yang patterns. A mass in this region would raise Blood stasis instead.

distractorExplanations.B: Liver Blood deficiency gives dizziness, blurred vision, numbness, and a thin pulse with a pale tongue, and does not produce subcostal resistance or distension worsened by stress.
distractorExplanations.C: Phlegm-Fluids in the chest give cough with thin sputum, chest oppression, and a slippery or wiry pulse, with fullness in the chest rather than tender resistance under the ribs that varies with emotion.
distractorExplanations.D: Spleen Qi sinking gives a bearing-down sensation, prolapse, and fatigue with a weak pulse; it does not produce hypochondrial resistance or a wiry pulse.

learningObjective: Interpret subcostal resistance and tenderness as a sign of Liver Qi stagnation.

stem: On palpation of a 62-year-old man's abdomen, the area below the umbilicus is soft, lacks tone and resilience, and feels empty, almost sinking under light pressure, while the upper abdomen has normal tone. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.A: Excess in the Lower Burner from Damp-Heat
options.B: Deficiency of the Kidney and the Lower Burner
options.C: Stagnation of Qi in the Lower Burner
options.D: Accumulation of Cold in the Lower Burner

explanation: The area below the umbilicus is the seat of the Kidney, Yuan Qi, and the lower Dan Tian. A lower abdomen that is soft, weak, and lacking resilience on palpation indicates deficiency of the Kidney and Lower Burner, often with deficient Yuan Qi. A firm, full, or tender lower abdomen would indicate Excess.

distractorExplanations.A: Damp-Heat in the Lower Burner is an Excess pattern that gives a full, tender, or hot lower abdomen with urinary or gynecological symptoms, not a weak, empty abdomen.
distractorExplanations.C: Qi stagnation produces distension and resistance that may move with pressure or passing gas; a soft, sunken, toneless lower abdomen is a deficiency sign.
distractorExplanations.D: Cold accumulation produces a cold, tight, or firm lower abdomen with pain relieved by warmth; lack of tone and resilience indicates deficiency rather than accumulation.

learningObjective: Interpret weakness of the lower abdomen below the umbilicus as Kidney and Lower Burner deficiency.

stem: A 57-year-old man reports a chronic cough. On palpation, the practitioner finds marked tenderness at the Back-Shu (Transporting) point area of the Lung on both sides and at the Front-Mu (Alarm) point area of the Lung on the chest, with no tenderness at the other Back-Shu points. Which interpretation of this finding is most appropriate?

options.A: A local channel obstruction confined to the back and chest muscles
options.B: A disorder of the Heart, since the chest is involved
options.C: A disorder of the Lung reflected at its Back-Shu and Front-Mu points
options.D: A disorder of the Bladder, since the Back-Shu points lie on its channel

explanation: The Back-Shu points on the back and the Front-Mu points on the chest and abdomen are where the Qi of each Zang Fu organ gathers, so tenderness, nodules, or changes in tissue at these points on palpation signal disorder of the corresponding organ. Tenderness at both the Back-Shu and Front-Mu of the Lung in a patient with chronic cough indicates a Lung disorder.

distractorExplanations.A: Tenderness confined precisely to the Lung Back-Shu and Front-Mu areas, in a patient with a Lung symptom, is an organ reflection rather than a purely local muscular problem; local obstruction would not select both the back and chest points of the same organ.
distractorExplanations.B: The Heart has its own Back-Shu and Front-Mu points; tenderness at the Lung points reflects the Lung, even though both organs lie in the chest.
distractorExplanations.D: Although the Back-Shu points lie on the Bladder channel, each one reflects the organ for which it is named; tenderness there is a diagnostic sign for that organ, not for the Bladder.

learningObjective: Interpret tenderness at Back-Shu and Front-Mu point areas as a diagnostic sign of the corresponding organ.

stem: A 66-year-old woman reports weakness and aching along the front of the lower leg for several months. On palpation along the Stomach channel on the leg, the skin feels cool, the muscle is flaccid and the tissue seems sunken and lacking in tone, with no nodules or sharp tenderness. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.A: Heat in the channel from Wind-Heat invasion
options.B: Blood stasis obstructing the channel
options.C: Damp-Heat pouring downward into the channel
options.D: Deficiency of Qi and Blood in the channel

explanation: Channel palpation assesses temperature, texture, and tissue quality. Coolness, flaccidity, and sunken, toneless tissue along the course of a channel indicate deficiency of Qi and Blood (or Yang) in that channel, with insufficient Qi to warm and fill the tissues. Excess conditions show the opposite: heat, swelling, hardness, nodules, or sharp tenderness.

distractorExplanations.A: Heat in a channel makes the skin warm or hot to touch, often with redness or swelling; coolness excludes Heat.
distractorExplanations.B: Blood stasis in a channel is shown by fixed sharp tenderness, nodules, cord-like thickening, or dark discoloration; the absence of nodules and tenderness with soft, sunken tissue indicates deficiency.
distractorExplanations.C: Damp-Heat pouring downward produces swelling, heaviness, and heat in the leg with a yellow greasy coating; cool, flaccid tissue is the opposite finding.

learningObjective: Interpret coolness and flaccid, sunken tissue along a channel as deficiency of the channel.

stem: A 64-year-old woman has swelling of both lower legs. When the practitioner presses a thumb into the swelling over the shin for several seconds, a depression remains after the thumb is removed and only slowly fills in. Which interpretation of this finding is most appropriate?

options.A: Water edema from Yang deficiency failing to transform fluids
options.B: Qi edema from stagnation of Qi
options.C: Phlegm accumulating in the muscles
options.D: Wind-Water with Lung Qi failing to disperse

explanation: Pitting edema, in which a depression remains after pressure and refills slowly, indicates accumulation of water in the tissues (water edema, shui zhong), most commonly from Spleen and Kidney Yang deficiency failing to transform and transport fluids, especially when it affects the lower legs in a chronic course. Non-pitting swelling that springs back at once indicates Qi edema (qi zhong) from Qi stagnation, or Phlegm.

distractorExplanations.B: Qi edema from Qi stagnation is non-pitting: the swelling rebounds immediately when pressure is released and often varies with emotion or time of day.
distractorExplanations.C: Phlegm in the muscles forms localized firm, non-pitting swellings or nodules rather than diffuse pitting edema of both legs.
distractorExplanations.D: Wind-Water is an acute pattern beginning in the face and eyelids with exterior symptoms; chronic bilateral pitting edema of the lower legs indicates Yang deficiency rather than Wind invasion.

learningObjective: Differentiate pitting edema (water edema) from non-pitting edema (Qi edema) on palpation.

distinction.key: Pitting that slowly refills is water edema (Yang deficiency); immediate rebound is Qi edema (Qi stagnation).

stem: A 45-year-old patient with a six-week history of afternoon fever has skin that feels warm on first touch. When the practitioner's hand rests on the skin for a longer period, the heat becomes more pronounced rather than fading, and the patient has night sweats and a red tongue with little coating. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.A: Heat in the exterior from Wind-Heat invasion
options.B: Heat in the Qi level from Yang Ming Excess
options.C: Dampness trapping Heat in the muscles
options.D: Heat in the interior from Yin deficiency steaming outward

explanation: Palpation of skin temperature distinguishes the depth of Heat. Heat that is strongest on initial touch and lessens with sustained pressure is in the exterior, whereas heat that increases the longer the hand stays on the skin comes from the interior, the Heat steaming out from the deep level. Combined with a six-week afternoon fever, night sweats, and a red tongue with little coating, this indicates Empty Heat from Yin deficiency (bone-steaming heat).

distractorExplanations.A: Exterior Wind-Heat gives acute fever with aversion to wind, and the skin heat is strongest on first touch and diminishes with sustained pressure; a six-week course with increasing heat on sustained touch indicates interior Heat.
distractorExplanations.B: Yang Ming Excess Heat gives high fever, profuse sweating, great thirst, and a dry yellow coating with an overflowing pulse; a red tongue with little coating and night sweats indicate deficiency Heat.
distractorExplanations.C: Dampness trapping Heat gives a lingering low fever with heaviness, a greasy coating, and skin that may feel warm but moist and sticky; the peeled red tongue and night sweats point to Yin deficiency.

learningObjective: Interpret the change in skin heat with sustained palpation to localize Heat to the exterior or interior.

distinction.key: Skin heat that intensifies with sustained touch is interior Heat; heat that fades with sustained touch is exterior Heat.

stem: A 30-year-old man is seen on the fourth day of a febrile illness. His hands and feet are cold to the touch up to the wrists and ankles, yet his chest and abdomen feel hot, he is thirsty for cold drinks, restless, constipated, with scanty dark urine. The tongue is red with a dry yellow coating. The pulse is deep, rapid, and forceful. Which interpretation of the cold limbs is most appropriate?

options.A: Yang deficiency failing to warm the extremities
options.B: Exterior Cold constricting the channels of the limbs
options.C: Interior Heat trapping Yang so that it fails to reach the limbs
options.D: Blood deficiency failing to fill the vessels of the limbs

explanation: Cold limbs with a warm or hot trunk is a key palpatory distinction. When Yang is deficient, the whole body including the trunk is cold. When the limbs are cold but the chest and abdomen are hot, with thirst for cold drinks, constipation, dark urine, a red dry tongue, and a deep, rapid, forceful pulse, interior Heat has trapped the Yang inside so it cannot reach the extremities (True Heat with False Cold, a Heat jue). The trunk temperature and the pulse reveal the true nature.

distractorExplanations.A: Yang deficiency produces coldness of the whole body including the trunk, with a pale tongue and a slow, forceless pulse; the hot trunk, red tongue, and forceful rapid pulse exclude it.
distractorExplanations.B: Exterior Cold gives chills over the whole body with a floating tight pulse and a thin white coating; the deep pulse and interior Heat signs exclude an exterior pattern.
distractorExplanations.D: Blood deficiency gives cold hands with a pale complexion, pale tongue, and thin pulse; the Heat signs and forceful rapid pulse rule it out.

learningObjective: Differentiate cold limbs from Yang deficiency from cold limbs due to interior Heat trapping Yang by palpating the trunk and limbs.

distinction.key: Cold limbs with a hot trunk and a forceful rapid pulse is Heat trapping Yang; cold limbs with a cold trunk and a forceless slow pulse is Yang deficiency.

stem: A practitioner compares the temperature of a feverish patient's forehead with that of the palms by touch. The forehead is distinctly hotter than the palms. According to the classical palpation rule, this finding most commonly indicates which of the following?

options.A: Heat in the interior from Yin deficiency
options.B: Heat in the Blood level
options.C: Heat from retention of Food in the Stomach
options.D: Heat in the exterior from invasion of a pathogenic factor

explanation: Comparing the forehead with the palms helps distinguish exterior from interior Heat. When the forehead is hotter than the palms, the Heat is in the exterior, as in Wind-Heat invasion. When the palms are hotter than the forehead, the Heat is in the interior, typically from Yin deficiency (five-palm heat). The forehead reflects the exterior and the palms the interior.

distractorExplanations.A: Interior Heat from Yin deficiency shows palms hotter than the forehead, with five-palm heat worse in the evening.
distractorExplanations.B: Heat in the Blood level shows high fever at night, bleeding, a deep-red tongue, and a rapid pulse; the forehead-versus-palm comparison is a rule for exterior versus interior Heat, and it points to the exterior here.
distractorExplanations.C: Retention of Food gives a hot, distended epigastrium with foul belching and a thick greasy coating; it is an interior condition and would not make the forehead hotter than the palms.

learningObjective: Apply the forehead-versus-palm temperature comparison to differentiate exterior from interior Heat.

distinction.key: Forehead hotter than palms is exterior Heat; palms hotter than forehead is interior Heat.
